# Harbour registry

A [Harbour](https://github.com/aryamurray/harbour) registry: a git repository holding real C and C++
packages as **pins and patches** (no upstream source is vendored). Packages are built from upstream's source
by a manifest written here; the one reviewed exception is a [prebuilt package](#prebuilt-packages). It is built to be maintained by
machines as well as by people, so everything a package is, and everything a package is judged by, is a
plain file in this repository, and the index Harbour reads is rendered from those files and checked.

## Use it

In Harbour's global config (`~/.harbour/config.toml`; a non-empty `registries` list REPLACES the
built-in registries, so keep those after it):

```toml
[[registries]]
name = "personal"
url = "https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>"   # or ssh://git@github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git
priority = -10                              # lower wins
```

Harbour fetches with your system `git`, so a private repo works with whatever your git is already set up
for (credential helper, `gh auth setup-git`, ssh keys). Then `harbour add zlib`.

## How it is organised

`packages/` is the **source of truth**. `index/` is **rendered** from it and committed, because Harbour
reads the git repository's `index/` directly (`harbour registry index` is how that tree is produced; there
is no server). `tools/render.py --check` fails CI if `index/` is not exactly what `packages/` produces.

```
packages/<name>/
  package.toml     identity, upstream, releases, test contract
  Harbour.toml     the manifest Harbour builds the package with (what the patch adds)
  overlay/         optional: extra files added to the upstream tree (vendored config header, generator scripts)
  patches/         optional: real fixes to upstream files, as *.patch
  test/            the consumer test: Harbour.toml + src/..., or run.sh for packages needing a custom driver
index/             rendered; never edited by hand
  <l>/<name>.idx                  tier-1 index: one JSON line per version (deps, checksum, license, shim path)
  <l>/<name>/<version>.toml       tier-2 shim: the source pin (tarball url + sha256 + strip_prefix, or git rev;
                                  for a prebuilt package one archive url + sha256 per platform) and its patches
  <l>/<name>/<version>.patch      git patch that ADDS Harbour.toml and the overlay files to the upstream tree
  <l>/<name>/<version>-<fix>.patch   one per patches/*.patch, applied first
tools/             render, lint, test, plan, guard (Python 3.11+ standard library only)
.github/           CI, and the action that installs the pinned Harbour
.harbour-version   the harbour commit CI builds and tests against
CODEOWNERS         the judge (tools/, .github/, packages/*/test/, .harbour-version) belongs to a human
```

A simple package and a complex one:

```
packages/zlib/                          packages/cpython/
  package.toml                            package.toml
  Harbour.toml                            Harbour.toml
  test/                                   overlay/harbour/{config.sh,freeze1.sh,freeze2.sh,pyconfig.sh,empty.c}
    Harbour.toml                          overlay/harbour/pyconfig/{linux-aarch64,linux-x86_64,macos-aarch64}.h
    src/main.c                            test/{run.sh,expected-frozen.sha256,consumer/}
```

### `package.toml`

`packages/_template/package.toml` is the annotated reference. In short:

| table | keys |
| --- | --- |
| `[package]` | `name` (= directory), `description`, `license` (SPDX, the upstream's), `homepage` |
| `[upstream]` | `git` (where tags are listed; the clone url for `rev` releases), `tag` (template), `url` (tarball template), `strip_prefix` (template), `scheme`; the watcher's policy `watch`, `max_bump`, `prereleases` (see [Keeping packages current](#keeping-packages-current)). A prebuilt package has `[[upstream.archive]]` entries instead of `url`/`strip_prefix` (see [Prebuilt packages](#prebuilt-packages)) |
| `[[release]]` | `version` (semver), exactly one of `sha256` (tarball), `rev` (git commit) or `archives` (prebuilt: a table of one sha256 per platform), `license_sha256` (the digest of upstream's license files at that release, required on the newest release; see [License drift](#license-drift)), optional `upstream_version`, `url`, `strip_prefix`, `republish` |
| `[test]` | `platforms` (`linux`/`macos`/`windows`), `objects` (exact translation-unit count: an integer, or `{ default = N, linux = N, "linux-x86_64" = N }`; `0` for a header-only or prebuilt package), optional `needs`, `timeout`, `verify` |
| `[review]` | `generators = true`, required when the build runs code (see below); `prebuilt = "<reason>"`, required when the package links upstream's binary instead of building upstream's source |

Templates expand `{version}` (upstream's spelling), `{major}`, `{minor}`, `{patch}` (from the semver) and,
in `url`/`strip_prefix`, `{tag}`. Unknown keys and placeholders are errors.

### Prebuilt packages

The registry's rule is that a package is **built from upstream's source** by a manifest written here. Some
libraries cannot sensibly be: libtorch's build generates most of its own sources, vendors dozens of
dependencies and takes hours, and upstream publishes official binaries per platform that every other package
manager consumes. Harbour links such a library as a `kind = "prebuilt"` target (its `MANIFEST.md`, "Prebuilt
Libraries"), and a registry entry for one carries **one archive per platform**, of which a build downloads only
its own.

**The trust rule.** A prebuilt package *trusts upstream's binary, pinned by sha256*. Nothing here compiles it,
so nothing here can say what is in it: the pin only guarantees that every user gets the bytes that were
reviewed. It is therefore allowed only as a deliberate, reviewed exception:

* `package.toml` must say `[review] prebuilt = "<why this cannot be built from source>"`. `lint.py` refuses a
  release with `archives`, or a manifest with a `prebuilt` target (`prebuilt_libs`/`runtime_libs`), without it,
  and refuses the flag on a package that has nothing prebuilt. `[review]` is a table an automated PR may never
  change, and CODEOWNERS can route it.
* **Every prebuilt release is a human's.** `tools/guard.py` refuses an automated PR that adds, changes or
  removes `archives` on any release (and `[[upstream.archive]]`, being part of `[upstream]`), and the watcher
  does not bump prebuilt packages at all.

**The schema.** Where the binaries come from is stated once, per platform, as templates (the same placeholders
as a tarball's `url`); each release then pins one sha256 per platform:

```toml
[upstream]
git = "https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch"     # optional, informational: the watcher does not follow it
tag = "v{version}"
watch = false

[[upstream.archive]]                            # one per platform upstream publishes a binary for
os = "linux"                                    # linux | macos | windows
arch = "x86_64"                                 # x86_64 | aarch64
url = "https://download.pytorch.org/libtorch/cpu/libtorch-shared-with-deps-{version}%2Bcpu.zip"
strip_prefix = "libtorch"                       # optional: the archive's single top-level directory

[[upstream.archive]]
os = "macos"
arch = "aarch64"
url = "https://download.pytorch.org/libtorch/cpu/libtorch-macos-arm64-{version}.zip"
strip_prefix = "libtorch"

[[release]]
version = "2.15.0"
license_sha256 = "..."                          # written by `watch.py license-digest`, as for any release
[release.archives]                              # "<os>-<arch>" = sha256 of that platform's archive
linux-x86_64 = "f26d7550..."
macos-aarch64 = "9fb883c4..."

[test]
platforms = ["linux", "macos"]
objects = 0                                     # nothing is compiled for the package

[review]
prebuilt = "cannot be built from a manifest; upstream's official binaries are what everyone ships"
```

`render.py` turns that into a shim with one `[[source.archive]]` per platform (`os`, `arch`, `url`, `sha256`,
`strip_prefix`, in `[[upstream.archive]]` order) and an `.idx` record with `format_version` 2, which a Harbour
from before prebuilt packages refuses by name. The record's checksum is `archives-sha256:<hex>`, one digest
over every platform's entry and the patches, so a lockfile written on Linux pins the macOS archive too. The
archive format is told from the URL's file name (`.zip`, `.tar.gz`, `.tgz`, `.tar.xz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar`). The
manifest (`Harbour.toml`, added by the patch as for any package) is the same for every platform: its
`[[targets.NAME.when]]` blocks name each platform's `prebuilt_libs` and `runtime_libs`, and it must be derived
from what upstream ships *inside the archives* (their CMake package, their libraries' own dependency tables),
not from memory.

What `lint.py` requires of a prebuilt release: an archive for **every platform in `[test] platforms`**, for the
architecture CI tests that platform on (`CI_ARCH` in `tools/regtools.py`: linux x86_64, macos aarch64, windows
x86_64), so a platform is claimed only where upstream publishes a binary; a 64-hex sha256 each; https URLs that
name the version; no platform and no URL twice; none of a source release's fields (`sha256`, `rev`, `url`,
`strip_prefix`, `[upstream] url`); every target `prebuilt` (or header-only) and `[test] objects = 0`. An archive
for a platform that is not claimed may stay listed (users on it can still install the package; CI just does not
test it).

**Bump a prebuilt package** (by hand; there is no bot path): add a `[[release]]` above the old one with the new
`version` and a `[release.archives]` table holding the sha256 of each platform's archive (`curl -fsSL <url> |
sha256sum`, the URL being the template with the new version), run `python3 tools/watch.py license-digest <name>
--write` (it downloads every archive and checks each against its pin), set `[package] version` in
`Harbour.toml`, and **re-derive the manifest's library lists from the new archives** (list each one's `lib/`;
upstream adds and drops bundled libraries between releases). Then render, lint and test as usual.

### Several versions of one package

`Harbour.toml` and `overlay/` describe **the newest release** (the highest semver in `[[release]]`). The
index is **append-only for older versions**:

* `render.py` rewrites only the newest release's shim and patches. Older releases stay listed in
  `package.toml` (it is the history) and their rendered files stay in `index/` exactly as published; the
  tool only *checks* them (shim present, the pinned sha256/rev matches `package.toml`, each patch hashes to
  what its shim lists) and carries their `.idx` record over.
* A release with no rendered files that is not the newest is an error: nothing keeps an old release's
  manifest, so it cannot be rendered later. Add releases newest-first, one at a time.
* `render.py --check --base <ref>` (what the PR workflow runs) additionally fails if any shim or patch that
  exists at `<ref>` differs now: a published version is immutable, because users' lockfiles pin the patch's
  sha256. Rewriting one on purpose (say, to fix a manifest) is a human decision recorded as
  `republish = "<reason>"` on that `[[release]]`, which stays visible in review and counts only in
  the pull request that adds or changes it (afterwards it is a record, not a standing exemption); the automated-PR guard
  refuses it for bots outright.

### Versions that are not semver

Harbour requires semver. `version` is always semver; when upstream's spelling differs, put it in
`upstream_version`, and `{version}` in templates then expands to that. `lint.py` checks
`normalize(upstream_version) == version`, so the mapping is reproducible (`render.py --normalize-version X`
prints it):

| upstream | `version` |
| --- | --- |
| `2024-12-28` (date) | `2024.12.28` (leading zeros dropped) |
| `2.10`, `7` | `2.10.0`, `7.0.0` |
| `3.0.0-rc1`, `3.0rc2` | `3.0.0-rc.1`, `3.0.0-rc.2` |
| `1.6.2.1` (four parts) | `1.6.2001`, only with `[upstream] scheme = "four-part"` |

The four-part rule folds the last component into the patch (`A.B.(C*1000+D)`, `D < 1000`) because
build metadata (`1.6.2+1`) is ignored by semver ordering, so `1.6.2.1` and `1.6.2` would tie. It applies to
every release of a package that declares the scheme (`1.6.3` becomes `1.6.3000`), never to some. Any other
shape is refused until `normalize_version()` in `tools/regtools.py` is extended on purpose.

## Add a package

1. `cp -r packages/_template packages/<name>` and replace every `example`.
2. **`package.toml`**: name, description, the upstream's SPDX `license`, `[upstream]` templates, one
   `[[release]]` with its `sha256` (of the exact tarball: `curl -fsSL <url> | sha256sum`) or a git `rev`.
   (A library that cannot be built from source at all is a [prebuilt package](#prebuilt-packages): per-platform
   archives instead, and `[review] prebuilt`. It is the exception; try a manifest first.)
   Then `python3 tools/watch.py license-digest <name> --write` adds the release's `license_sha256` (it downloads
   the pinned source, checks the hash, and digests upstream's license files; do not write it by hand).
3. **`Harbour.toml`**: the manifest. Name every source file (a source list that silently shrinks still
   links). `[package] version` and `license` must equal the newest release's. Dependencies are other packages
   in this registry, by version.
4. **`test/`**: a consumer that depends on the package *through the registry* and asserts real behaviour,
   printing `OK ...` as its last line. Start from `packages/_template/test` or a sibling package's.
5. `python3 tools/render.py` to render `index/` (and the README table), then `python3 tools/lint.py`.
6. `python3 tools/test.py <name>` with a `harbour` on `PATH` (or `--harbour BIN`). Set `[test] objects` to the
   count it reports, after checking the number is what the library should compile.
7. Commit `packages/<name>/` and the rendered `index/`, open a PR. CI re-checks all of it on every
   platform you listed.

## Bump a version by hand

1. Add a new `[[release]]` above the old one in `package.toml` (`version`, `sha256` or `rev`). Keep the old entry.
   `python3 tools/watch.py license-digest <name> --write` adds its `license_sha256`; if that differs from the old
   release's, upstream's license files changed: read them, and correct `license` (here and in `Harbour.toml`) if needed.
2. Set `[package] version` in `Harbour.toml` to the new version; fix the manifest and `overlay/` if the new
   release needs it (new source files, a regenerated vendored header).
3. `python3 tools/render.py && python3 tools/lint.py && python3 tools/test.py <name>`.
4. If the test fails because the library changed (a different source count, a renamed symbol) fix
   `Harbour.toml`; if `[test] objects` is now legitimately different, update it: that is a human edit.
   The old version's rendered files must show no diff.

## The quality bar

A package is in the registry when, on every platform in its `[test] platforms`:

* its **license** is an SPDX expression on the allowlist (`tools/lint.py`; `LicenseRef-*` is allowed for
  licenses SPDX has no identifier for), and it equals the `Harbour.toml` license;
* its source is **pinned by hash** (tarball `sha256`, or full git `rev`) over https, and the package is
  **built from that source**. A [prebuilt package](#prebuilt-packages) is the reviewed exception: upstream's
  binary for each platform, each pinned by `sha256`, behind `[review] prebuilt = "<reason>"`;
* its newest release records **`license_sha256`**, re-derived from the pinned source by CI, so the next bump can
  tell whether upstream's license files changed;
* it **builds** through the registry with every source pattern matching a file (`--strict-sources`), a second build recompiles nothing, and the consumer **runs and prints `OK`
  as its last line** after asserting real behaviour (round trips, known answers, a server answering commands),
  including that the library reports the version `package.toml` declares;
* it compiles **exactly `[test] objects` translation units**, because a source list that silently shrinks still
  links and still passes. (A prebuilt package compiles none: `objects = 0`, its consumer still builds and runs
  on every claimed platform, and the test checks that the archive fetched is that platform's and that the
  lockfile carries the release's `archives-sha256:` checksum.)

Code that runs during the build (`prebuild`/`postbuild`/`recipe`, `host = true` targets, scripts in `overlay/`,
patches that add scripts) is allowed only with `[review] generators = true`, so a human sees the flag flip.
A binary that is linked instead of built (`archives` on a release, a `prebuilt` target) is allowed only with
`[review] prebuilt = "<reason>"`, for the same reason.
`lint.py` also refuses non-https URLs, credentials and secret-looking strings anywhere in a package, symlinks,
CRLF or binary overlay files, and a `[test] platforms` entry the manifest's `supports` excludes.

## The tools

All are Python 3.11+, standard library only, and run on Linux, macOS and Windows (Git Bash).

| tool | what |
| --- | --- |
| `tools/render.py [pkg...]` | render `packages/` into `index/` and the README table. `--check` fails (with a diff) if stale; `--check --base REF` also enforces append-only; `--harbour BIN` lets `harbour registry index` produce/verify the `.idx` files (downloads every package's source) |
| `tools/lint.py [pkg...]` | static checks, no network |
| `tools/test.py pkg... \| --all` | the consumer test, through the registry (below) |
| `tools/plan.py --base REF \| --all` | affected packages (changed + reverse dependencies from the `.idx` files; everything, in shards, if `tools/test.py`, `tools/regtools.py`, `tools/plan.py`, `pr.yml`, `.github/actions/`, `.harbour-version`, `.gitattributes` or `config.toml` changed) and the CI matrix |
| `tools/guard.py` | the automated-PR guard |
| `tools/rot_issues.py` | the nightly workflow's issue bookkeeping |
| `tools/watch.py list\|report\|bump` | the release watcher: find newer upstream versions, write the candidate bump (cross-checking the tarball's sha256, recording the license digest) |
| `tools/watch.py license-digest PKG [--write]` | compute the newest release's `license_sha256` from its pinned source (network) |
| `tools/watch.py verify-license --base REF` | re-derive every `license_sha256` a change adds or alters (network; the PR workflow's `License digests` job) |
| `tools/watch.py supersede --package P --version V` | close the open bump PRs that the open bump PR for `V` replaces |
| `tools/bump_triage.py` | what happens when the gate finishes on a bump PR (labels, one failure summary, repair budget) |
| `tools/repair.py` | the repair step: asks a language model (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, `REPAIR_*` settings) for a rewritten manifest and accepts only files inside its output contract. `--print-prompt` shows what would be sent without sending it |
| `python3 -m unittest discover -s tools -p "test_*.py"` | tests of the tools (the patch renderer against real `git diff`, the guard against real git history, lint, render and the watcher against mutated copies of the fixture registry in `tools/testdata/registry/`: synthetic `fx-*` packages, so that no change to a real package can fail the tools' self-test) |

### Rendering is byte-exact

A shim lists each patch with the sha256 of its exact bytes. `render.py` writes the text `git diff --binary`
prints for the added files (verified against git in the tests), the shim in the generator's format, and the
`.idx` lines in `serde_json`'s compact form. `.gitattributes` carries `*.patch -text` so line-ending
conversion cannot change a patch (`harbour registry index` insists on it). The built-in `.idx` renderer
ports what `harbour registry index` does for registry-only dependencies; CI's `Index` job runs the real
command over everything and fails if the two ever disagree.

### How `tools/test.py` works

It snapshots this checkout's `index/` into a throw-away git repository (Harbour clones registries with git, so
`file://<checkout>` would only see committed files), writes an isolated `HOME` whose
`~/.harbour/config.toml` has that snapshot as the **only** `[[registries]]` entry, copies `test/` to a scratch
directory, and runs `harbour build --strict-sources` (fetch, verify, patch, compile as a dependency) twice, then the consumer.
`--strict-sources` makes every pattern in `sources` and in each active `when` block match a file, so a pattern that
matches nothing is an error rather than a library that quietly shrank; a pattern that is legitimately empty on one
platform belongs in a `when` block for the platforms where it matches.
It requires exit 0, last non-empty line `OK` or `OK ...`, and the dependency's object count (excluding
probes and host tools) to equal `[test] objects` for the platform (`<os>-<arch>`, then `<os>`, then `default`).
For a prebuilt package (and a header-only one) that count is 0: nothing is compiled for the dependency, the
consumer's own sources still are, and the lockfile must pin the package from the registry. A prebuilt package
must additionally have an archive for this platform and architecture (none is a failure, not a skip), its
lockfile checksum must be the index record's `archives-sha256:` one, and the build output must name this
platform's archive as the one downloaded and no other platform's.
The consumer reads `REGISTRY_TEST_UPSTREAM_VERSION` and must check the library reports it.
A package not listing the current platform is skipped with a message. On failure the full log is printed.
(Windows cannot isolate `HOME`: Harbour asks the OS, not the environment, for the home directory, so there the
registry is selected with Harbour's `HARBOUR_TEST_REGISTRY_URL`.)

**`[test] verify = true`** adds a second, independent signal: `harbour verify <pkg> --registry-path <snapshot>
--format json --strict-sources`. It builds the newest release the way a consumer does, includes every public header
that compiles on its own, links a harness against the library (referencing one of its symbols) and runs it, and the
test fails if any stage fails; the harness level that ran is printed. It catches what a hand-written consumer does
not: a header that cannot be included, or a system library missing from the public link surface (it is how libpng's
missing `m` shows up without any consumer touching `pow`). It is opt-in because it is a second release-profile build,
roughly as long again as the test itself (about a minute for harfbuzz, which therefore leaves it off). The harness
is in the library's language, so for a C++ library it is C++ and says nothing about C consumers.

**`test/run.sh`** is the escape hatch for packages that are programs, not libraries (redis, cpython). It runs under
bash with cwd = a scratch directory and the same isolated registry. Environment: `HARBOUR`,
`REGISTRY_TEST_PACKAGE`, `REGISTRY_TEST_VERSION`, `REGISTRY_TEST_UPSTREAM_VERSION`, `REGISTRY_TEST_OBJECTS`,
`REGISTRY_TEST_PLATFORM`, `REGISTRY_TEST_DIR` (the package's `test/`), `REGISTRY_TEST_WORK`,
`REGISTRY_TEST_PYTHON`. It must build the package through the registry inside a project under
`REGISTRY_TEST_WORK` (a stub project depending on it: Harbour builds *every* target of a dependency, programs
included, under `.harbour/target/<profile>/deps/<name>-<version>/`), exercise it, exit 0 and print `OK ...` last.
The runner then applies the same last-line and object-count checks.

## CI

* **`pr.yml`** (`pull_request` only, read-only token, never `pull_request_target`): `guard` (automated PRs),
  `plan` (tool self-tests, lint, `render.py --check --base`, affected set and matrix), `license` (re-derives from
  the pinned source every `license_sha256` the PR adds or alters), `harbour` (build and cache
  Harbour per runner image), `index` (the authoritative `harbour registry index` check), `test` (one leg per
  affected package and platform; a change to what builds and tests packages re-tests everything, packed into a few
  shards per platform), and **`PR result`**, the one check to require in branch protection.
* **`watch.yml`** (every 6 hours, manual, and `workflow_run` of `PR`): the release watcher and what follows a
  failed bump PR; see [Keeping packages current](#keeping-packages-current).
* **`nightly.yml`** (weekly and manual): every package on every platform; a failure opens or comments on ONE
  `rot` issue per package, and the issue closes when the package passes again.
* Harbour comes from `.harbour-version` (a commit SHA), built with `cargo build --release --locked` and cached per
  SHA/OS/arch by `.github/actions/setup-harbour`. When Harbour has releases, only that action changes.

### The bot-PR guard

This is the safety property of the autonomous loop the registry is built for: **the judge cannot be modified by
the judged.** A PR is automated if its author login ends in `[bot]`, its user type is Bot, it carries the
`bot` label, or its head branch starts with `bot/` (the watcher's `bot/bump-<package>-<version>`; the branch is
needed because a `pull_request` event carries the labels the PR had when it fired, and a PR opened through the
API and labelled a moment later is seen by its first run as unlabelled). An automated PR may change only `packages/*/package.toml`, `packages/*/Harbour.toml`,
`packages/*/overlay/**`, `packages/*/patches/**` and `index/**` (plus the generated README table). It may not
touch `packages/*/test/**`, `tools/**`, `.github/**`, `.harbour-version` or `CODEOWNERS`; may not change a
`package.toml`'s `[test]`, `[review]`, `name`, `license`, anything in `[upstream]` (where the source comes
from, and the watcher's policy `watch`, `max_bump`, `prereleases`) or a release's `republish`; may not add,
change or remove the `archives` of any release (the pinned binaries of a [prebuilt package](#prebuilt-packages);
their URLs are in `[upstream]`); may not add a package; and may only *add* version
files under `index/` (a published version is immutable). `tools/guard.py` implements it and is tested against real
git history.

Because a bot may not change `license`, the guard also holds the rule that makes a relicense visible
([License drift](#license-drift)): an automated PR may not add, change or remove the `license_sha256` of a
release that already exists; a release it adds must carry one; and that digest must **equal** the digest of the
newest release on the base branch. A different digest (upstream's license files changed), or no digest to compare
with, is refused: that bump is a human's.

What makes it hold, beyond the job: CODEOWNERS puts `tools/`, `.github/`, `packages/*/test/` and
`.harbour-version` under a human, and the repository must enable *Require review from Code Owners*, require
the `PR result` check, and keep the bot account out of the bypass list. A `pull_request` workflow runs the
PR's own copy of itself, so a PR that deletes the guard job is only stopped by that branch protection; the
guard's script is therefore fetched from the base commit.

## Keeping packages current

The loop: **detect** an upstream release, **bump** the entry, let **the PR gate** (everything above) judge it,
**merge**. When the carried-forward manifest no longer builds, a **repair** step asks a language model to propose
a rewritten one, which is committed to the same PR and judged by the same unchanged gate. The repair step is off
until you give it a model endpoint (below); it has not yet been run against a real model or on GitHub.

```
watch.yml  detect --> bump (one PR per package, newest version) --> pr.yml gate --> merge
                                                                        |  red
                                                  triage: label, ONE summary comment, attempt counter
                                                                        |
                                       repair (model proposal) --commit to the same branch--> pr.yml again
                                                                        |  budget spent
                                                              `needs-human` label + issue, stop
```

### How detection works

`tools/watch.py list` prints, per package, the newest `[[release]]` and the newest upstream stable version;
`report` is the same as JSON (the workflow's matrix). Nothing needs a token or the GitHub API:

* `[upstream] git` is asked for its tags with `git ls-remote --tags` (https only, no prompts, a timeout).
* `[upstream] tag` is the template the registry already uses to build a release's tag. It is **inverted**:
  `v{version}`, `{version}`, `curl-{major}_{minor}_{patch}`, `VER-{major}-{minor}-{patch}`... become a regular
  expression, and every tag that matches is normalised to semver with the same `normalize_version` the lint uses
  (so `2024-12-28`, `2.10` and a package's `scheme = "four-part"` work). A tag is only accepted if expanding the
  template with the version derived from it gives back **exactly that tag**: a version the registry could not
  reproduce is reported, never invented (`zlib`'s `v1.3.1.2` is the example).
* Ordering is semver precedence, not text. Pre-releases (`rc`, `alpha`, `beta`) are skipped unless
  `prereleases = true`. A package whose upstream is *older* than the registry is never downgraded.
* Packages pinned by git `rev` (libpng, freetype, harfbuzz) resolve the tag to its **commit**. `ls-remote` is run
  *without* `--refs` for this reason: an annotated tag's own id is the tag object, and the commit is only on the
  peeled `refs/tags/X^{}` line (harfbuzz's `15.0.0` is annotated; the registry's `rev` is the peeled one).
* A package with no `[upstream] git` or `tag`, with `watch = false`, a [prebuilt package](#prebuilt-packages)
  (per-platform archives: never bumped by the watcher, whatever `watch` says), or a tarball release with no
  `[upstream] url`, is reported as `not watchable: <why>`; an unreachable host is an `error` row. Neither stops
  the others.

**Policy** (keys of `[upstream]`; **human-owned**: `tools/guard.py` refuses a bot PR that changes them):

| key | effect |
| --- | --- |
| `watch = false` | opt the package out entirely |
| `max_bump = "patch"` / `"minor"` / `"major"` | the biggest jump the watcher follows from the current version: patch releases of the current minor, minor and patch releases of the current major (the default), or any newer stable version. A version held back is reported, not bumped |
| `prereleases = true` | also follow rc/alpha/beta tags |

One PR is one package and one version: the newest allowed, not every intermediate one. **Major releases are held back by default**
(redis 7 -> 8, openssl 3 -> 4): that is where the things the gate cannot see change, such as the API a dependent
package was written against. (A license change is no longer one of them, at any version distance: see
[License drift](#license-drift).) Set `max_bump = "major"` on a package to let the watcher
follow them, or bump a major by hand. A package versioned by date (`2024-12-28`) follows every release by default,
since its "major" is only the year.

### The candidate: `watch.py bump PKG [--to VERSION]`

* **tarball packages:** builds the URL from the templates, downloads it (https only, redirects must stay https,
  256 MiB cap, timeout, hashed while streaming; the archive is only *listed*, never extracted), records the
  `sha256`, and checks the archive's top-level directory against `strip_prefix` after templating. A wrong prefix
  fails with what the archive actually contains. The sha256 is then
  [cross-checked](#cross-checking-the-sha256) against what upstream publishes.
* **git-rev packages:** sets `rev` to the commit the tag points at.
* **both:** records `license_sha256`, the digest of upstream's license files at the new release
  ([License drift](#license-drift)).
* Adds a `[[release]]` at the top of `package.toml` by **textual insertion** (comments and layout are untouched;
  the result is re-parsed and compared with the old file plus exactly one release), changes only the
  `[package] version` line of `Harbour.toml` the same way, and leaves `overlay/` and `patches/` byte-identical.
  `upstream_version` is added when upstream's spelling is not the semver. Then `render.py` runs for the package.
* Self-check before it finishes: the result is judged by `tools/guard.py` as a bot PR, by `lint.py`, and by a
  stricter rule (only `package.toml`, `Harbour.toml`, the README table and that package's `index/` may differ).
  If anything fails the working tree is rolled back. The tree must be clean when it starts. (When the license
  digest changed, the guard's refusal for that reason, and only that one, is expected.)
* Per-release `url` / `strip_prefix` overrides on the previous release are not carried forward (the templates
  are used); the prefix check catches a mismatch.

### License drift

A bump carries `[package] license` forward unchanged, and the bot may not edit it. Without more, an upstream
relicense (redis 7.2 is BSD-3-Clause; 7.4 and 8 are not) would merge with a green gate. So every release records
what upstream's license files looked like:

```toml
[[release]]
version = "1.3.1"
sha256 = "9a93b2b7..."
license_sha256 = "3cb8e028..."     # digest of upstream's license files at this release
```

* **What is digested.** The files at the top level of the source (after `strip_prefix`) named `LICENSE*`,
  `LICENCE*`, `COPYING*`, `COPYRIGHT*` or `UNLICENSE*` (any case; the bare name or the name followed by `.`, `-`
  or `_`; not source files such as `license.h`), and every file directly inside a top-level `LICENSES/`. Each
  file's text is normalised (every year, and run or range of years, becomes `YYYY`; whitespace is collapsed) and
  hashed; `license_sha256` is the sha256 of the sorted lines `<file sha256>  <path>`. So a new copyright year, a
  re-wrapped paragraph or CRLF endings change nothing; any change of wording, and any license file added, removed
  or renamed, changes the digest. A link is recorded as its target, not followed. `tools/watch.py license-digest
  PKG` prints the files and the digest.
* **A prebuilt release** is digested over **all** of its archives: each one's top-level license files, listed
  as `<os>-<arch>/<path>`. Computing or verifying it downloads every platform's archive and requires each to
  hash to its pin, so the `License digests` job is also where all of a prebuilt release's sha256s are checked
  (a test job only ever downloads its own platform's). Official binary archives often carry no license file
  at all (libtorch's do not); the digest is then that of the empty list, which can only show one appearing.
  `license` for such a package is what upstream's *source* repository states; say so in `package.toml`.
* **How it is read.** From the tarball's members, in memory (1 MiB per file, 64 files; nothing is extracted), or,
  for a git-pinned release, from the tag's tree, fetched into a throw-away bare repository (https only, no hooks,
  no checkout) and read with `git cat-file`.
* **What the watcher does with it.** The new release gets its digest. When it equals the previous release's, the
  PR body says "license files: unchanged". When it differs, the candidate is still written and the PR still
  opened, but **for a human**: its body leads with the change (old and new digest, the files found), it is
  labelled `needs-human` and `license-changed`, and **auto-merge is not requested for it**, whatever
  `REGISTRY_AUTO_MERGE` says.
* **What the gate enforces.** Two things, so that this does not rest on the watcher behaving:
  1. `tools/guard.py` refuses an automated PR whose new release does not carry exactly the digest of the newest
     release on the base branch, and refuses any automated change to an existing release's digest. A
     license-changed bump PR is therefore **red** (`PR result` fails on the guard) and cannot merge, by auto-merge
     or by a click. Triage leaves it alone (it is already `needs-human`; no repair attempt is spent on it).
  2. The `License digests` job of `pr.yml` (`watch.py verify-license`) re-derives, from the pinned source, every
     `license_sha256` a pull request adds or alters, and fails on a mismatch. A bot PR cannot pass by copying the
     previous digest forward: the digest it records has to be the one the source it pins really has.
* **What the human does.** Read upstream's license at the new tag. Then take the bump over in a PR of your own:
  the same commit on a branch outside `bot/` without the `bot` label (for example `gh pr checkout <n> && git
  switch -c bump-<pkg>-<version> && git push -u origin HEAD`, then open the PR and close the bot's), changing
  `license` in `package.toml` and `Harbour.toml` if it did change. Human PRs are not restricted by the guard; the
  new release's digest becomes the baseline for the next bump.
* **Limits.** It sees the license *files*, not license headers inside sources, a `NOTICE`, or a license that
  lives only in a README or below the top level. A source with no license file at its top level gets the digest
  of an empty list (the PR says so), which can only show a license file *appearing*. Years are deliberately
  ignored. A package whose newest release has no `license_sha256` is reported as `not watchable` until a human
  records one, and `lint.py` requires it on every package's newest release.

### Cross-checking the sha256

The `sha256` a bump records is the hash of what the job downloaded. Where upstream publishes a digest of its own,
`watch.py bump` compares before it writes anything:

| source | when | what agreement is worth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the asset's `digest` in GitHub's releases API (`api.github.com/repos/<o>/<r>/releases/tags/<tag>`) | the tarball is a GitHub release asset, and it was uploaded after GitHub began recording digests | the strongest available: computed by GitHub at upload and fetched from another host than the download. It rules out a corrupted or substituted download; it does not vouch for whoever uploaded the asset |
| a checksum asset of the same release (`<tarball>.sha256`, `SHA256SUMS`, `checksums.txt`, ...) | such an asset exists and names the tarball | weaker: same uploader, same host. A corrupted, truncated or swapped download, not a compromised host or account |
| `<tarball url>.sha256` | any host that serves one | the same, weaker kind |

* A source that **disagrees fails the bump** (the job is red, nothing is pushed, the error shows both hashes).
  Every source found is checked; one agreeing source does not outvote a disagreeing one.
* When a source agrees, the PR body says `sha256 cross-checked, agrees with ...`, naming the source and what it is
  worth, and the bump commit's message says which kind it was.
* When there is none, or it cannot be reached (rate limit, outage), the PR body says **`sha256 not
  cross-checked`** and why. Unreachable is never treated as agreement, and it does not fail the bump.
* Same network rules as the download: https only, redirects must stay https, a size cap (4 MiB), a timeout;
  nothing is executed. The API call may carry the job's **read-only** `GITHUB_TOKEN` (anonymous runners are
  rate-limited); it is sent to `api.github.com` only and no redirect is followed with it.
* Git-pinned packages have nothing to cross-check: a commit id is its own content hash. Signatures (`.asc`,
  `.sig`, sigstore) are not verified.

### The workflow, and the token you must create

`.github/workflows/watch.yml`: `detect` (read-only) -> `bump` matrix (`max-parallel: 2`; fast checks, guard, push
`bot/bump-<package>-<version>`, open a PR labelled `bot` + `bump` that states the package, old -> new, the
upstream compare URL when upstream is on GitHub, the new sha256 or rev, and "manifest carried forward
unchanged", whether the sha256 was cross-checked, and whether the license files changed) -> `triage` and `repair`
for a failed gate. Manual runs take a `package` and a `dry-run` input
(dry-run writes and checks the candidate and pushes nothing). A package with an open bump PR for the same or a
newer version, or an open `needs-human: <package> <version>` issue, is skipped; a leftover branch is not reused.

**A superseded bump PR.** When upstream releases a newer version while an older bump PR of the same package is
still open, the watcher opens the newer bump and then closes the older PR with **one** comment pointing at the
replacement, and deletes its branch. It does that only to a PR that is provably nothing but its own work:

* the head branch is exactly `bot/bump-<package>-<older version>`, **in this repository** (not a fork);
* it carries the `bot` and `bump` labels and does **not** carry `keep`;
* **every commit** on it has the watcher's author *and* committer email
  (`harbour-registry-watch@users.noreply.github.com`, `BOT_COMMIT_EMAILS` in `tools/watch.py`), the list is
  complete (under 250) and ends at the PR's head;
* it was opened by the same account as the replacement PR (the bot token's).

Anything else (a person pushed a commit or edited a file in the web UI, someone added `keep`, the commits cannot be
listed) and the watcher **waits**, as it used to, until that PR merges or is closed: a person is working there, and
a second PR would only race them. `detect` makes that decision before a bump starts; the bump job checks again,
from live state, after the replacement PR exists, and closes nothing when no replacement is open. The branch is
deleted only if it still points at the commit that was checked. If closing fails after the replacement was opened,
the next run finishes it and does not comment twice. To keep a bump PR open on purpose, label it `keep` or push a
commit of your own. (A commit made by a later automated step under another identity, such as a repair commit,
counts as "not the watcher's" until its email is added to `BOT_COMMIT_EMAILS`: the PR is then kept, not closed.)

**The token problem.** A PR opened with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not trigger `pull_request` workflows, so
the gate would never run on it. Two designs were weighed:

1. **Built:** the PAT/app token. `secrets.REGISTRY_BOT_TOKEN` pushes the branch and opens the PR, so `pr.yml` runs
   normally and `PR result` appears as a real check that branch protection and auto-merge can use.
2. **Not built:** open with `GITHUB_TOKEN` and `workflow_dispatch` `pr.yml` on the branch. It would need `pr.yml`
   to get its author, labels and base from dispatch inputs, which are exactly what the guard judges with, set by
   whoever dispatches; and the results would be runs on the branch, not PR checks, so required-check branch
   protection and auto-merge could not wait on them. That is a weaker, more complex gate.

Without the secret the `bump` job **fails immediately**, with instructions. Detection and dry runs need no secret.

What to create:

| what | value |
| --- | --- |
| secret `REGISTRY_BOT_TOKEN` | a fine-grained PAT (or GitHub App installation token) scoped to this repository only: Contents read+write, Pull requests read+write, Issues read+write (for labels). Only the push, label, PR, supersede (comment on, close and delete the branch of a bump PR that a newer one replaces) and auto-merge steps see it; keep that account **out of the branch-protection bypass list** |
| variable `REGISTRY_AUTO_MERGE` | `true` to run `gh pr merge --auto --squash` on each bump PR, **except one whose upstream license files changed** (never requested for those). Default off. Needs "Allow auto-merge" in the repository settings and `PR result` required by branch protection; otherwise it is a warning and the PR waits for a human. **Nothing in the workflow merges anything itself.** Flip it once you trust the gate |
| variable `REGISTRY_REPAIR_ENABLED` | optional **off switch**. Repair is on by default, declared in the triage job of `watch.yml`. Set this **repository** variable to `false` and a failed bump goes straight to `needs-human` |
| variable `REGISTRY_REPAIR_ATTEMPTS` | repair attempts per bump PR, default `2` |
| environment `Openrouter` | a GitHub environment (Settings > Environments). Only the `repair` job declares it, so what it holds can be read by that job and by nothing else in the repository. Do not add required reviewers (every repair would wait for approval); restricting it to the default branch is fine |
| secret `OPENROUTER_KEY`, **in that environment** | the OpenRouter key, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Only the one step that calls the model sees it |
| variable `OPENROUTER_BASE`, **in that environment** | the API base, `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`: the URL up to and including the version segment, https only. The repair step POSTs to `<base>/chat/completions` and contacts nothing else |
| the model | not a setting: `openai/gpt-oss-20b` is written in the `repair` job of `watch.yml`, so changing the model that rewrites manifests is a reviewed change to that file |
| variables `REPAIR_TEMPERATURE`, `REPAIR_MAX_TOKENS`, `REPAIR_TIMEOUT`, `REPAIR_TOTAL_TIMEOUT`, `REPAIR_MAX_PROMPT_CHARS` | optional; see below |
| labels `bot`, `bump`, `needs-repair`, `needs-human`, `license-changed`, `keep`, `repair-attempt-N` | created by the workflow when missing. `keep` is the one a person applies (a bump PR carrying it is never closed as superseded) |

Branch protection that makes this safe (already required by the guard section above): require `PR result`,
require Code Owners review, and `bot/**` is treated as automated by the guard (`bot` label or a `bot/` head branch).

### When the gate fails: triage and the repair seam

On `workflow_run` of `PR` completing for a `bot/bump-*` branch of this repository, the `triage` job
(`tools/bump_triage.py`) labels the PR `needs-repair`, posts or edits **one** comment (which package x platform
jobs failed, the log lines leading up to each failure, the upstream compare stat and added/removed/renamed files
when upstream is on GitHub), and counts attempts in `repair-attempt-<n>` labels, incremented *before* the repair
job starts so a crashed repair still spends its attempt. A green run removes `needs-repair`/`needs-human`. When
repair is not enabled or the budget is spent: label `needs-human`, drop `needs-repair`, open the issue
`needs-human: <package> <version>`, stop. The job starts seconds after the run ends, when GitHub may not have
finished storing a job's log: a log that is not there yet is asked for again a few times (bounded), and if it
never comes the summary carries the reason (the HTTP status) in place of the log lines.

**Security of that job.** `workflow_run` runs the default branch's workflow in the base repository with write
permissions, after a workflow that executed PR code. So it checks out the default branch only and never the PR's
sha or ref; runs only `tools/` from that checkout; reads run metadata and logs through the API; takes every string
that came from the PR through environment variables (never `${{ }}` inside a `run:`), validates the branch name
against a strict regex and quotes log text in a code fence the text cannot close; ignores runs from forks and
non-`pull_request` events; uses the job's own token (labels, comments, issues; no contents write); and approves or
merges nothing.

**The repair contract** (`tools/repair.py`; its docstring is the full text):

* *input:* the failure summary, the upstream added/removed/renamed file listing, the diff text of upstream's own build files (CMake, Makefile, meson and the like, capped), the run context, and the bump
  branch's `packages/<pkg>/` fetched as data into a directory (never executed);
* *output:* files for `packages/<pkg>/Harbour.toml`, `overlay/**`, `patches/*.patch`, nothing else (files can be
  added or rewritten, not deleted), committed to the **same** bump branch with `REGISTRY_BOT_TOKEN` so `pr.yml`
  judges it again unchanged. `validate_output` is the single authority on paths, size and encoding; the manifest
  must also parse as TOML, keep its `[package] name` and `version`, and differ from what the branch has;
* *budget:* `REGISTRY_REPAIR_ATTEMPTS`, then `needs-human`. Inside one attempt the model is called at most three
  times: a refused reply is sent back with the reasons twice, then the attempt fails;
* *the model* is told that upstream source, changelogs and logs are untrusted data, runs with no secret but its own
  scoped key, has no tools (one request, one text reply; nothing is executed), and its output is only ever applied
  as file content inside the allowed paths. The judge (tests, `[test]`, tools, workflows) is outside those paths
  and CODEOWNERS-protected. This is what bounds a prompt injection: the worst a hostile changelog can obtain is a
  wrong manifest, which the gate then refuses.

**What the model is sent.** One system message (the task, the manifest concepts it needs, the rules, the reply
format) and one user message with five delimited data blocks: the carried-forward `Harbour.toml` (never cut),
`package.toml` (reference only), the failure summary, the upstream file changes, and the package's overlay and
patch files. The upstream listing is pre-digested: files the manifest names that upstream removed or renamed come
first, then new files in directories whose sources the manifest lists one by one. Each block's delimiter carries a
tag derived from the content, so text inside a block cannot close it. Sizes are capped; anything trimmed is
trimmed the same way every time and the prompt says so. To read exactly what would be sent, without sending it:

```
python3 tools/repair.py --package PKG --input-dir DIR --candidate-dir DIR --print-prompt [FILE]
```

**What the model must answer.** Marker lines, alone on their line, with paths relative to `packages/<pkg>/`; text
outside the blocks is ignored, any other `=== ... ===` line or an unterminated block refuses the whole reply:

```
=== EDIT: Harbour.toml ===              exact search/replace on an existing file (preferred: small, and the
<<<<<<< SEARCH                          rest of the file cannot be damaged). SEARCH must match exactly one
    "lib/old_name.c",                   run of whole lines.
=======
    "lib/new_name.c",
>>>>>>> REPLACE
=== END ===

=== FILE: overlay/config/extra.h ===    or the complete content of a file
...
=== END ===

=== CANNOT REPAIR: one line saying why ===
```

**Pointing it at a provider.** Any service or local server that implements the OpenAI chat-completions request
(`POST <base>/chat/completions` with `model` and `messages`, the reply in `choices[0].message.content`) works; no
vendor SDK is involved and nothing but the Python standard library is used.

1. In the GitHub environment `Openrouter` (create it if it does not exist), store the OpenRouter key as the
   secret `OPENROUTER_KEY` and set the variable `OPENROUTER_BASE` to `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`.
2. The model is declared in the `repair` job of `.github/workflows/watch.yml` (`REPAIR_MODEL`).
   It is a named model (`openai/gpt-oss-20b`), billed to the OpenRouter account, so the same model answers
   every repair. OpenRouter's free router (`openrouter/free`) was tried first: on the first real repair its
   choice took twenty minutes and returned no text. To use another provider, change what the job maps to `REPAIR_API_BASE`,
   `REPAIR_API_KEY` and `REPAIR_MODEL`.
3. Optional variables: `REPAIR_TEMPERATURE` (default `0`), `REPAIR_MAX_TOKENS` (reply tokens, default `8192`;
   either accepts `omit` for providers that reject the field), `REPAIR_TIMEOUT` (seconds of wall clock per request, default `300`), `REPAIR_TOTAL_TIMEOUT` (seconds for the
   whole attempt, every round and retry, default `900`),
   `REPAIR_MAX_PROMPT_CHARS` (default `150000`; lower it for a model with a small context window. A prompt is
   about a quarter as many tokens as characters; curl's is about 32,000 characters).
4. Nothing to switch on: repair runs by default. To stop it, set the repository variable
   `REGISTRY_REPAIR_ENABLED` to `false`.

With the key or the base missing (or the environment misnamed, which GitHub creates empty), the repair job fails with "not configured: set ...",
and the PR is handed to a human. To try a provider before enabling anything, export the three variables in a
shell and run `tools/repair.py` on a directory laid out as above; `http://localhost` is accepted as a base for a
local model server.

**The `repair` job.** Default branch checked out; the bump branch fetched as data (and skipped if it has moved
since the triaged run). Then three steps that never share credentials: *propose* (the only step with the model
key; no GitHub token; the process starts from an emptied environment), *apply* (no secret: re-verifies the output,
copies it over the branch's package, runs the **default branch's** `render.py`, commits as the bot, and refuses
the commit unless `git diff --name-only` stays inside `packages/<pkg>/Harbour.toml`, `overlay/**`,
`patches/*.patch` and that package's `index/` files, and `tools/guard.py` passes), and *push* (the only step with
`REGISTRY_BOT_TOKEN`; not a force push). The model's replies are kept as the `repair-transcript` artifact, not
printed. If nothing is pushed, the job labels the PR `needs-human` and opens the issue itself, because without a
new commit there is no new gate run to triage.

**What repair cannot fix, by design.** `package.toml` and `test/` are the judge. When a release changes the number
of translation units (`[test] objects`) or the behaviour the consumer test asserts, the best possible manifest
still fails the gate and the PR ends at `needs-human` with the manifest already corrected. curl 8.22.0 -> 8.23.0 is
such a case: three sources removed, two renamed and two added makes 195 objects against a declared 196.

### Not built

* The repair step has never run against a real model or on GitHub Actions: the model call is tested against a
  local fake endpoint and the `repair` job's scripts were run by hand. It cannot delete files, and it sees the
  upstream file *listing*, not upstream file contents (GitHub's compare lists at most 300 files).
* Verifying upstream **signatures** (`.asc`, `.sig`, sigstore). The sha256 cross-check covers published digests
  only, and for hosts that publish none (python.org, download.redis.io, dist.libuv.org today) a bump still records
  the hash of what was downloaded and says "not cross-checked".
* License drift below the top level: license headers in sources, `NOTICE` files, a license stated only in a README.
* Showing *which* license file changed, or a diff of it, in the PR (only the old and new digest and the new file
  list are known; the previous release's per-file hashes are not stored).
* Closing the `needs-human: <package> <version>` issue of a bump PR that was closed as superseded.
* Binary overlay files and `.idx` yanking are not supported by the tools yet.
* Automatic bumps of prebuilt packages (a new version means one new archive and sha256 per platform, each
  downloaded and cross-checked, and a manifest re-derived from the new archives); `env` (`gnu`/`musl`/`msvc`)
  and `format` on an archive entry, which Harbour's shim accepts and `package.toml` cannot yet say; and license
  drift for binaries whose archives carry no license file (see [License drift](#license-drift)).
